readerTitle: Why higher cigarette taxes cut smoking and still raise more money
caseNote: 실제 정책·연구 (미국 2009년 연방 담뱃세 인상, World Bank·IARC 탄력성 연구) + 실제 기업 (Philip Morris의 1993년 'Marlboro Friday') + 가상 적용 (사내 IT팀, 식용유 유통업체)
insight: 가격 탄력성은 하나의 평균값이 아니다. 기존 충성 고객은 버티고, 신규·가격 민감 고객은 떠나며, 그 차이는 시간이 갈수록 커진다.
misconception: 중독성 있거나 꼭 필요한 제품은 가격을 올려도 아무도 반응하지 않는다. 전체 판매량이 거의 안 줄었으면 가격 인상은 공짜다.

sources.text: World Bank (1999). Curbing the Epidemic: Governments and the Economics of Tobacco Control. 고소득 국가 가격 10% 인상 시 소비 약 4% 감소, 저·중소득 국가는 더 큼
IARC Handbooks of Cancer Prevention, Vol. 14 (2011). Effectiveness of Tax and Price Policies for Tobacco Control. 청소년·저소득층의 높은 가격 반응, 장기 반응이 단기보다 큼, 세율 인상 시 세수 증가
US Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau / CHIPRA (2009). 연방 담뱃세 갑당 $0.39 → $1.01 (2009년 4월 1일 시행)
Philip Morris의 Marlboro 가격 인하 발표 (1993년 4월 2일, 'Marlboro Friday') 당시 언론 보도 (예: The New York Times, 1993년 4월 3일)

factChecks.note: 탄력성 수치: World Bank(1999)는 고소득 국가에서 가격 10% 인상 시 소비 약 4% 감소, 저·중소득 국가는 약 8%로 제시. IARC(2011)도 고소득 국가 대략 -0.2~-0.6 범위로 요약. 카드에는 'roughly 4%'와 'often more in poorer countries'로만 적었습니다. 게시 전 원문 확인 필요.
미국 연방 담뱃세 인상: CHIPRA(2009)로 갑당 39센트에서 $1.01로 인상, 2009년 4월 시행, 아동 건강보험 재원 마련 목적. 정확한 시행일과 금액 재확인 필요. 인상 후 실제 흡연율·세수 변화 수치는 카드에 넣지 않았습니다.
청소년·저소득층이 가격에 더 민감하고 장기 반응이 단기보다 크다는 내용은 IARC(2011) 결론. 구체적 배수는 연구마다 달라 카드에 숫자를 넣지 않았습니다.
Marlboro Friday: 1993년 4월 2일 Philip Morris가 할인 브랜드에 맞서 Marlboro 가격 인하를 발표했고 주가가 하루 만에 크게 하락. 인하 폭(갑당 약 40센트)과 주가 하락률(약 20% 이상)은 자료마다 달라 카드에는 'sharply'로만 적었습니다.
3번 카드 계산(가상): 100갑 × $10 = $1,000. 가격 10% 인상 $11, 판매량 4% 감소 96갑. 96 × $11 = $1,056, 즉 +5.6%. 세수가 아닌 총 지출 기준 단순화 예시입니다.

cards.title: Why higher cigarette taxes cut smoking and still raise more money
body: Governments raise cigarette taxes for two reasons: to get people to smoke less, and to raise money.
Those goals sound like they fight each other. If people quit, the tax money should vanish. Yet in country after country, both tend to happen at once.

image.label: A cigarette pack with a growing tax stamp beside a rising coin stack
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 상표 없는 흰 담뱃갑 위 세금 스티커가 점점 커지는 3단계 모습, 옆에는 동전 더미가 점점 높아짐. 실제 담배 브랜드 로고나 디자인은 절대 쓰지 않음. 흡연 장면 미화 금지.

cards.title: The tax on a pack almost triples.
body: In 2009, the US raised its federal cigarette tax from 39 cents to $1.01 a pack, partly to fund children's health insurance.
Smokers are hooked, and the money was meant to keep flowing. Based on decades of research, what usually happens when cigarette prices jump?

options.text: Smoking barely changes because smokers are addicted, so revenue jumps
options.feedback: Half right. Revenue does tend to rise, but smoking falls too. Assuming nobody reacts hides the people who quietly do.

options.text: Smoking falls modestly, mostly among young and lower-income people, and revenue still rises
options.feedback: That's the usual pattern. Most buyers stay, so the money grows, while the most price-sensitive groups cut back or never start.

options.text: Smoking drops so much that tax revenue falls
options.feedback: That happens only when demand is very sensitive to price. For cigarettes overall, it usually isn't, so revenue tends to rise.

cards.title: Price up 10%, packs down about 4%.
body: Big reviews by the World Bank (1999) and the WHO's cancer agency, IARC (2011), found that in high-income countries a 10% price rise cuts cigarette use by **roughly 4%**, often more in poorer countries.
Fewer packs, more money. Simple illustrative numbers:

cards.title: The average hides who's moving.
body: That "4%" is an average. Inside it, groups react very differently. Long-time heavy smokers barely change. **Young people and lower-income smokers** cut back much more, and many would-be smokers never start.
This is **elasticity by segment**: how strongly each group of customers responds to a price change. One market can hold a loyal core that pays almost anything and an edge that walks away fast.

image.label: Crowd split into a steady core and a shrinking edge
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데에 움직이지 않는 진한 색 사람 아이콘 무리('Long-time buyers'), 바깥쪽에 흐려지며 빠져나가는 연한 색 아이콘들('Young', 'Low income', 'Would-be starters'). 위쪽에 가격 화살표가 올라가는 모습. 담배 그림 없이 추상적으로.

cards.title: The effect grows over time.
body: The first year after a tax rise shows only part of the story. Quitting takes time, and the biggest change comes from people who never pick up the habit.
IARC's review found that the long-run response to price is larger than the short-run one. A small dip in year one can become a much bigger gap a decade later.
So the loyal core keeps paying today, while the market slowly shrinks from the edges.

cards.title: The same split shows up inside companies.
body: An internal IT team starts charging departments for cloud storage to rein in costs. Total storage drops only a little, and the charge brings in a steady budget.
But look closer. Data-heavy teams with real needs keep paying. Small teams delete old files, and new projects pick cheaper tools. The average looks calm. The edges are already moving.

cards.title: Steady demand for the category isn't steady demand for you.
body: Higher cigarette prices also push smokers toward cheaper brands, roll-your-own tobacco, cross-border shopping and smuggled packs. Some of the "lost" sales just move elsewhere.
Philip Morris learned this in the early 1990s. As premium prices kept rising, discount brands gained share. On April 2, 1993, the company cut Marlboro's price, and its shares fell sharply that day.
Buyers may never leave cigarettes. They can easily leave **one brand**.

image.label: Shoppers sliding from a premium shelf to a discount shelf
image.brief: 상점 진열대 두 칸. 위쪽 고급 칸에서 쇼핑객 아이콘들이 화살표를 따라 아래쪽 저가 칸으로 이동. 전체 사람 수는 그대로라는 점을 강조. 실제 브랜드 로고·포장 디자인 사용 금지.

cards.title: Now it's a cooking oil distributor.
body: You supply cooking oil to restaurants and corner shops. Three months ago you raised prices 8%. Total volume fell only 2%, and revenue is up.
Your sales team says the increase worked. What do you do next?

options.text: Call it a success and plan another 8% rise
options.feedback: The total looks fine, but it may hide price-sensitive customers already leaving. A second rise can turn a quiet loss into a fast one.

options.text: Break volume down by customer type and track new accounts before deciding
options.feedback: You keep the gain and learn who is drifting away. If small shops or new accounts are falling off, you can protect them before the gap grows.

options.text: Roll the increase back in case anyone leaves
options.feedback: Safe for small customers, but you give up margin from loyal buyers who clearly accept the price. Better to find out who is reacting first.

cards.title: After a price rise, look past the average.
body: A small drop in total sales can hide a loyal core that stays and an edge that leaves, and that edge grows over time.
**Try it today:** take your last price change. Split the sales response by customer type and by new versus existing customers. Who moved?
